How to fill it in

What a statement of work is for

A statement of work (SOW) records exactly what one party will deliver to another, by when, for what price and how it will be accepted. It sits under a master services agreement or contract, or it can stand alone for small jobs. Its purpose is to prevent the arguments that start with “I thought that was included”.

Step 1: Name the parties and the project

Replace the provider and client names, the reference and the date, and give the project a clear name. If a master agreement already exists, add its title and date in the summary so the SOW refers to it. Keep a version number and update it each time you change the document.

Step 2: Say what is in scope and what is not

In the summary, write one sentence for the scope and a list of what is excluded. Exclusions matter more than most people think: hosting, content, licences, travel, training, support after go-live. Whatever is not written down is a likely argument, so name it. Anything later added goes through change control.

Step 3: Make every deliverable checkable

Each deliverable needs three things: what it is, what form it takes and how it is accepted. “Working system delivered to a test environment; accepted when all agreed test cases pass” can be checked. “High-quality solution” cannot. Number them D1, D2 and so on, tie each to a phase and use the numbers in the pricing table so there is one list of truth.

Step 4: Build a realistic timeline

Set start and end weeks for each phase and a milestone the client must accept. Phases may overlap, but the milestones should not. Include client dependencies: if you need data, access or feedback, say when and who. Late client input should move dates by the same number of days; put that in the assumptions.

Step 5: Price the scope

The sample has three scopes: Core, Standard and Full. If you have only one scope, keep a single fee and delete the extra columns. Use your own numbers and state whether the fees include VAT or sales tax. Tie payments to milestones, for example 30% on signature, 40% on build complete and 30% on handover accepted, so the client pays for results.

Step 6: Terms and signatures

The terms table lists the acceptance procedure, change control, payment terms, intellectual property, confidentiality and governing law as placeholders. These are legal questions and depend on your country and contract: ask a solicitor or attorney to complete them or point to your master agreement. Both parties sign and date; keep a signed copy.

Before you send

Search for square brackets and delete or complete each one, check that weeks and fees agree throughout and read the acceptance section as if you were the client. For a version that sells the work with options, use the consulting proposal template, and see the proposal and SOW guide.

Common mistakes to avoid

Common SOW problems are vague deliverables, no acceptance process, silent assumptions and no change control. A deliverable such as “support” with no hours, response time or end date is a dispute waiting to happen. If the client does not respond to a deliverable within the agreed window, say what happens: many SOWs treat silence as acceptance after a stated number of days. Be careful with fixed fees for fuzzy scope; if the scope is unclear, price a discovery phase first and then fix the fee for the rest.

Frequently asked questions

Is this statement of work template free?

Yes. Download the Word and PDF files without an email address.

Is a SOW a legal contract?

It can be, once both parties sign, but it is usually read together with a master agreement. This template is not legal advice. Have a lawyer complete the terms.

What is the difference between a SOW and a proposal?

A proposal persuades; a SOW fixes the agreed scope. See the proposal template.

Can I use it for a time-and-materials job?

You would need to change the pricing section to rates and an estimate. The scope, deliverables and acceptance sections still apply.

Is it A4 or Letter?

A4. In the US, change Layout > Size to Letter in Word and check the tables.
